entities.name: Church of Iceland
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Iceland (Þjóðkirkjan — 'People's Church'), established as a Lutheran state church in 1550 following the Reformation (imposed after the beheading of Catholic Bishop Jón Arason — the last Catholic bishop in Scandinavia to resist the Reformation) and still legally the 'national church' of Iceland today (though with reduced state privileges), is the dominant religious institution in one of the world's most secular societies — with 65% of Iceland's 370,000 people as registered members but only 2-3% attending weekly services. Iceland's simultaneous high church membership and low religiosity makes it a paradox of Nordic secularism.

Bishop Jón Arason (1484-1550) was the last Catholic bishop in Scandinavia and the last major opponent of the Lutheran Reformation — he had twice been excommunicated and twice reconciled with Rome. After Danish King Christian III imposed Lutheranism across his domains, Jón Arason was captured without trial and beheaded at Skálholt in 1550 with two of his sons — the last beheadings in Icelandic history and the effective end of Catholicism in Iceland for 400+ years.

The Church of Iceland's modern character: it ordained women from 1974 (relatively early among established European churches); a woman, Ingibjörg Sigurðardóttir, served as Bishop of Iceland 2012-2023; same-sex blessings approved 2010; same-sex marriages performed from 2014. Despite these progressive stances, Iceland is consistently ranked among the world's least religious countries by belief surveys, with a majority of Icelanders identifying as non-religious despite church membership.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Iceland — established through the last Catholic bishop in Scandinavia's beheading in 1550 and now serving 65% of the world's least religious country — encapsulates the full arc of Scandinavian Lutheranism: from violent imposed Reformation to culturally nominal progressive Christianity.
